Sketch is an open-ended series. Works evolve as I code a generative project, sometimes drastically. Intermediate works usually don't see the light of day - they get archived and forgotten. This series is snapshots of different forms along the way - each standing alone, but also part of a larger meandering work flow. The word Sketch implies incompleteness. This project may end up being two works, or it could evolve for years. Part of the joy of generative art is never knowing what's around the corner. I have no set schedule. There may be multiple Sketches released a week, or it could be weeks or months between drops. I have no idea where Sketch is heading and there is no guarantee of cohesiveness from Sketch to Sketch. Color palettes and forms will change as new ideas are explored.

17776.d:
This project is about uncovering artifacts.

Each piece is determined by approximately 15 parameters. This allows for a multitude of possible forms, and each iteration is an artifact to be discovered within the multidimensional space.

This work is focused around discovery. It is about exploring the space of the algorithm, shedding light on its many forms, and sometimes finding artifacts of the real world embedded within them.

Technically, this work is a composition of three primary elements: Voronoi tessellations, orthographic projection, and the depth-sort algorithm.
The latter of these is integral to the rendering mechanism. It works intuitively, drawing distant objects before near objects, evaluating the distance of each object according to its geometric center. It does this precisely, and in doing so, it can produce interesting visual artifacts, drawing some shapes in an unexpected order.



This has been a fascinating study, bringing light to unreal shapes and forms, and uncovering artifacts in an impossible space.

I hope you enjoy it,
Nat Sarkissian

Summer, 2022 I had 2 (physical) art exhibitions in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Both exhibitions combined physical and digital work, including NFT's. 'Sharding' explores the creation and destruction of generative knot, and related, geometries. The facetted geometry is creating utilizing the following steps:
1. curve creation
2. form extrusion
3. Verlet node creation
4. facetted face creation

The different steps enable the forms to be disassembled/reassembled into their face primitives, including accurate (enough) collision response.

CircuTiles project is a set of tiles with patterns created just by using circles. 
There are many circular shapes in our real world, so by different arrangement of circles beside each other’s, there you can find  familiar images, like human body, figures, animals, clouds, sun, waves and many more.

Color pallet: In this project I've used my specific color pallet which consists of 11 color sets and each color set contains 6 colors. two of these color sets are in grayscale. Basically I extract these colors from nature pictures and after using them on each piece calibrate them mostly by changing in brightness and saturation in HSB color mode to have the best output.

In this work, you can find 6 general different patterns:

These sections are:

1- Minimal: using minimal concept, in which here you can see this concept by using just black and white colors (just black and white background and lines) and using very little number of circles in each tile.

2- Gray, using just a gray color and using more iteration of shapes than minimal pattern.

3- Single color, just like step 2, while replacing gray with one of the colors from my color pallet.

4- Gradient color, using a color gradient with one-color tone and also using more iterations of shapes in each tile.

5- Mixed colors, in this series, each drop used all colors in one of the color sets.

6- Wireframes and simple movement, in the final pattern, all tiles have one same color as background and all circles have no fill color but have colorized frames. Also, some specific tiles have simple movements.

Cityblocks: Genesis

In the Cityblocks series, urban ensembles are generated with a simple click. With each iteration appears a new densely built city block. Graced with impeccable geometrical lines, devoid of any human presence, these buildings remind us of brutalist utopias like Le Corbusier’s Cité radieuse or Niemeyer’s Brasilia. But despite their clearly modernist feel, there is something hauntingly primitive about them. They could be either New Mexican adobe pueblos, Minoan palaces, or Turkish troglodyte dwellings. Both carved and sculpted, these Ghormenghasts of concrete float in a realm out of time, like in some architect’s dream.

The purpose of this creative work is to generate 3D architectural projects that could be implemented in the real world. The accelerating lives that we live, complicated by growing and unpredictable environmental crises, call for an enhanced capacity to come up quickly with new architectural solutions adapted to different contexts. From computer assisted design to 3D printing, from augmented reality to real-life housing, from sculpture to architecture, this work aims at bridging the gap between the virtual and the tangible.

Working as a visual artist, David Umemoto draws inspiration from his training as an architect. He has been using low-tech methods for a long time, refining his talent for elegant simple shapes and combinatory constructions. Now, poured concrete and home-made moulds are giving way to zero-gravity rotating models. The skills he developed while working with real objects find a new playground in the virtual realm.

All of our strong emotions, feelings and experiences come from childhood. Sincere happiness or frightening cruelty is primarily inherent in children, so they learn about the world. When we were children, we first hurt someone, first burst into tears from resentment, learned what is good and what is bad. 
Our parents did not answer our questions, either because they did not know the answer or because they thought we were too young. We learned to look for the answers ourselves. Whoever says that children don't understand is a fool. They do understand, but they do it in their own way. The world as seen through the eyes of a child is not like the world as seen through the eyes of an adult. It is often not built on the laws of physics or the laws of the marketplace. In a child's world or universe, the moon is just a little light in the sky, and the next street is already a different country. Their world is built on speculation and magical theories. Unfortunately, a child's world is not eternal. As they grow up, the "real" life, the life of adults, pokes into them like a sharp needle over and over again. 
There is something incredibly tragic about this time gap between child and adult. It is this period that I wanted to trace in my work. As teenagers, it is as if we are between two trains, we are no longer children, but we are not yet adults. We get to know ourselves, we test our strength and readiness to exist in the "real" world. We are trying to find our place in the unfriendly world of adults, but we are also not ready to let go of the magic of childhood. It confuses, torments, and frustrates us. But it is a necessary and unavoidable tragedy.

The only time I ever received corporal punishment – something that was still legal in schools during the 1970s – was in Double Maths with Mrs Robinson. The log book spread out before me seemed less appealing than talking with my friends at the back of the classroom, and so it was I found myself, palm outstretched, feeling the whack of Mrs. Robinson's ruler, ten times over. "Math sucks." Or so I thought.

Back then I knew nothing of the beauty that I would later see in Mathematics – something which became apparent as I taught myself to code, especially using Processing.

This work – based on code I've been playing around with since 2009 – is my small homage to that beauty. Originally based on Ulam spirals, I've then played around with that starting formula to create an infinite numbers of patterns using square roots, cosines and modulus. If only they had shown me these possibilities when I was younger I may have avoided the dreaded ruler of Mrs. Robinson.

Originally developed as an experiment of recreating rolls of thread in p5js, this collaboration of efforts combines se.nao.neste's core algorithmic work with Liam's drive to push as much coherent variety into a generator as possible.

At its core, this work wraps threads around a central point, subscribing to various rules as it does so. The movement of the thread is determined by the angular momentum combined with a "wander" factor.

One of the most exciting parts of the development of this algorithm was discovering and exploiting the various idiosyncracies (the peculiarities) of the drawing algorithm - the broken lines when the stroke is above a certain weight, the "burning" of the heavily layered shadows etc. - these "mistakes" we've loved and cherished and became an intrinsic part of the artistic expression of the piece.

A study of building and destroying. I built this. You may knock it over.

Humans are both creators and destroyers. One of the earliest games children learn to play is building with blocks, then knocking them down. This simple activity is teaching kids about gravity, cause and effect, and imposing their will on the world around them. As children grow older, the gap between these opposing actions widens. The intention behind knocking things down becomes less innocent, and creators aren't as excited to see their work destroyed.

In 1915, the Russian avant-garde founded the abstract art movement known as Constructivism, rejecting everything except for the absolute purest aspects of form and material. This art was used in service of the Russian revolution and utilized heavily in its propaganda, intended to highlight the utilitarian nature of industrial progress. Mainly, building the new Russia. Its influence is lasting, and can be seen throughout art and design trends even today.

When Russia invaded Ukraine in February of 2022, footage of missiles and airstrikes decimating Ukrainian buildings permeated the media. Ukrainian lives, kitchens, windowsill gardens, and family photos tumbled to the ground. Like children's blocks. Things that took a lifetime to build were destroyed in seconds. 

KONSTRUKTS represents this duality in creation and destruction. Stacked children's blocks are rendered in the style of Constructivist designs like El Lissitzky's Proun series, and Alexander Rodchenko's posters. With a simple tap, blocks (or buildings) can be knocked to the ground.

- Tap anywhere to reveal the KONSTRUKTS menu in the top left. Tap the menu for several options.
- KONSTRUKTS can be exported as USDZ or GLTF models to be used in augmented reality or the metaverse.

- If you knocked over the blocks, you can reset them from the menu.

KONSTRUKTS is built entirely with code, using Three.js, JavaScript, and GLSL.

Cyclical Cellular Automata (CCA) are a cousin of Conway's Game of Life. They're both 2D cellular automata, mathematical games that exhibit emergent behavior based on the interaction of discrete elements governed by a set of rules.

Each pixel in petriDish is a cell and its color represents its state. The rules governing how each cell changes its state is based on the cell's current state and the state of neighbors surrounding it. For a cell to advance to its next state, a number of its neighbors be in the next state. The size of the neighborhood and the number of neighbors included in the count, as well as the minimum number of neighbors in the next state comprise the rules that produce all of petriDish's behaviors.

The size of the pixels, color palette, number and state of rules, and neighborhood characteristics are unique to each piece and fixed at the time of minting.

Not all states will cycle forever. Some will halt or need a little nudge. Others you can play like a game. Simply click and drag to randomize a small region of states around your cursor.
